title: Storm Boelo leaves 90,000 without power as Met Office issues new wind warning
summary: A clean-up operation is under way in parts of the UK after Storm Boelo caused flooding and property damage, leaving thousands without power.

content:
A clean-up operation is under way in parts of the UK after Storm Boelo caused flooding and property damage, leaving thousands without power.

The Energy Networks Association (ENA) said around 90,000 properties are still without power as of Monday.

Two men were killed by falling trees during the storm on Sunday - a man in his 20s whose car was hit in north London and a 60-year-old in Mid Kelton, Dumfries and Galloway.

The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for strong winds from 18:00 on Monday to 03:00 on Tuesday across the west coast of England, Wales and Scotland and eastern parts of Northern Ireland.

The Met Office has warned that further power cuts in areas covered by the warning are likely and people should make sure they have essentials prepared, including torches and batteries.

Coastal communities could also be affected by spray or large waves, while travel delays are expected.

Boelo is the second storm to have hit parts of the UK in recent days, following Storm Austen.

Leo Slade, CEO of the ENA said it had been "a tough weekend" and that efforts to reconnect some properties were being hampered by the weather, with sustained winds of 50-85mph across parts of Scotland and northern England.

"Until that weather system passes, we can't safely get engineers out to replace poles, to get wires back up, so today is going to be a hive of activity in getting engineers out into the field," Slade told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

He stressed that the UK's power network was very resilient and money was spent to prepare for these sorts of scenarios, but said a debate was needed over how much more investment was required to mitigate for further storms brought by climate change.

Storm Boelo clears but more wind and rain bears down on UK

Published 51 minutes ago Marcus Reed, the operations director at a home fragrance manufacturer, said his factory and shop in Lyndal, Cumbria would be without power until Tuesday evening.

He told the Today programme that he has had to turn away employees and customers.

"To lose two days manufacturing and distribution is going to be really disruptive," he said, adding that it was bad timing as it was "the busiest time of the year" for his business in the lead-up to Christmas.

"This is probably the worst situation I've experienced in my time here; we've had ad hoc issues over weekends where we've lost power, but it's been contained within a 12-hour period. It's the first time anything like this has happened, it's very serious."

Wendy McKinney, whose bathroom shop in the seaside town of Largs in North Ayrshire was flooded on Sunday, told the Today programme the storm had been "devastating to local businesses".

She said the local council only handed out sandbags after flooding had already started:"[They] were just left in the middle of the street yesterday afternoon on pallets just for everybody just to try and help themselves, but it was too little too late."

North Ayrshire Council told the BBC that it had distributed almost 300 sandbags in Largs and Saltcoats and would continue to "respond where it has been safe and appropriate to do so".

A spokesperson said council teams "followed established resilience procedures" but would review flooding reports and "consider any lessons that can be learned".

Disruption to travel has continued on Monday, and some schools in Scotland have been shut either due to lack of power, heating, water or damage.

Another yellow warning of wind , external has been issued by the Met Office, covering much of Scotland, as well as parts of northern England and Northern Ireland from 03:00 to 23:59 on Tuesday.

Monday morning has seen rain in many parts of south-west England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and this is moving north-eastwards reaching central, eastern and northern England, as well as most of Scotland, by around lunchtime.

Winds will also strengthen throughout Monday, and it will turn even windier overnight as the area of low pressure passes close to Northern Ireland and north-west Scotland with gusts peaking on Tuesday.

title: How The Beatles found their drummer at Butlin's
summary: A Lincolnshire holiday camp played a little-known but crucial part in the birth of The Beatles.
key_takeaways: A Lincolnshire holiday camp played a little-known but crucial part in the birth of The Beatles.
A young, bearded Ringo Starr was playing drums with Rory Storm and the Hurricanes at the Butlins in Skegness in the summer 1962 when Paul Mc
Bobby Thomson, who was bassist in the Hurricanes, recalls the duo arriving early one morning after driving all night from Liverpool.
content:
A Lincolnshire holiday camp played a little-known but crucial part in the birth of The Beatles.

A young, bearded Ringo Starr was playing drums with Rory Storm and the Hurricanes at the Butlins in Skegness in the summer 1962 when Paul McCartney and John Lennon arrived to try and recruit him to the band.

Bobby Thomson, who was bassist in the Hurricanes, recalls the duo arriving early one morning after driving all night from Liverpool.

"I think that was the whole idea, to invite him to join the Beatles," he said.

"Because I was with Ringo they didn't come out with it. They could have, it wouldn't have bothered me."

He said that a few weeks later in mid August the band were having breakfast when an announcement over the speaker system asked Starr to report to reception.

He asked Thomson to come with him and the pair arrived to find a phone call from Beatles manager Brian Epstein asking if Starr would like to join the group.

Starr later recalled the conversation in an interview. "The boys would like you to join The Beatles. What do you say?

"I said, 'no, I'd love to, when?' And he said, 'oh, tonight'. I said, 'I can't', this was Wednesday, 'I can't come tonight. I'm in a band, I'll come Saturday'."

Thomson said that during the call with Epstein the drummer was told to lose his facial hair.

"He didn't want to shave his beard off," Thomson said laughing.

"So the beard came off and he got the haircut to match."

Madeline Morrison, who worked as a Redcoat at the Clacton camp, said people were surprised when the rumours of Starr joining The Beatles soon started to spread throughout Butlin's.

"I've got playbills where Rory Storm and the Hurricanes were above The Beatles."

She added people said he had been taken to the hairdresser: "He's got the Beatle haircut, he's joining them.

"You know, all this sort of stuff would jump round all the camps because we were all villages."

After Starr's departure Rory Storm and the Hurricanes recruited another drummer for the remaining two weeks of the summer season.

Another celebrity whose career began as a Butlin's Redcoat remembered occasionally sitting in on the drums for Starr.

Think of a Number TV presenter Johnny Ball said he would often play the first part of the Hurricanes' Sunday night performances.

"He [Starr] could flinch an extra hour on his day off if I stood in for him and played his first half of the gig," he said.

Soon after Starr joined the Fab Four, they had a UK hit with their first single Love Me Do and went on to make musical history around the globe.

Thomson described his former bandmate as "a smashing bloke"

"His personality and everything was spot on," he said.

Thomson added that in joining the Beatles "He actually made the whole team, the full set".

"We just knew that they were going to be absolutely huge."

"You were waiting for the talent to take the world over, which they did the following year."

Starr's only return to Lincolnshire with his new group would be their performance at the ABC cinema in Lincoln in November 1963.

Photographer Ken James remembered the experience as "absolute bedlam".

"The fans were screaming it was unbelievable," he said.

"The second they came on they were screaming, quite hysterical some of them."

content:
West of England political editor Published 19 October 2026 A woman who entered care at 14 says her foster parents gave her stability, love and a future she never thought possible.

The number of foster carers has fallen by 12% since 2021 while the number of children needing care continues to rise.

The government has initiated a campaign to get 10,000 more foster care places. Ministers are promoting regional fostering hubs set up in recent years, including in the South West.

"Fostering definitely saved my life. If I wasn't fostered I don't know who I'd have ended up with," said Amy Burns, who was there for the launch at Downing Street.

Published 7 days ago In Pictures: 'Lido's dog event' and 'world BBQ finalists'

Published 7 days ago Amy, now 26, and from Bristol, entered foster care at the age of 14 after what she describes as a difficult family situation.

Looking back, she believes the support and stability she received changed the course of her life.

"I had come out of a really bad family relationship, and if I hadn't been actually saved by my foster parents, I don't know where I'd have ended up.

"If they didn't stick it out, and if they didn't give me the love that I needed then I absolutely would not be here today."

Amy went on to attend university and build a career in the media, something she says would not have been possible without her foster family.

Amy's story comes as foster carer numbers fall and demand for placements grows.

The number of children in care in Bristol and Somerset has risen by 35% over the past seven years.

Experts say foster care often delivers better outcomes for children, but a shortage of carers means more young people are ending up in children's homes.

Amy was among the speakers at the launch of a new government initiative aimed at recruiting thousands more foster carers.

The campaign includes a push to attract people from a wider range of backgrounds and encourage more flexible forms of fostering.

Children and Families Minister Josh MacAlister said more people may now be able to consider fostering.

"Families can come forward in their 20s or 30s or 40s, who might be able to foster part-time at the weekends," he said.

"Now is the time to come forward and join fostering, because it is changing and it is improving."

Guidelines will be made clearer, helped by £88m of new funding.

Also backing the campaign is Wes, a single parent from Yate in South Gloucestershire, who has fostered and adopted children over the past 14 years.

Wes, 46, believes many people rule themselves out before finding out what fostering involves.

"I feel that every day I've made a chance for a child to have a better life," he said.

He said concerns about finances or the challenges children may bring should not necessarily stop people from applying.

"Yes there is trauma, and yes sometimes I have to talk about the past, but to me it's all about the day that you're in and what's coming forward, that child knows that they're going to be safe and happy in my care."

Among those supporting recruitment efforts is Jon Hubbard, Wiltshire Council's cabinet member for children's services.

His council plays a leading role in the South West Fostering Hub, which was set up two years ago to help councils work together on recruitment and support for foster carers.

He said the shortage of foster homes had practical as well as financial consequences because more children end up in residential care, where placements can be significantly more expensive - at £318,000 per year.

"I cannot stress enough: every foster carer we recruit not only makes a massive difference to a young person's life, but also actually saves a considerable amount of money," he said.

title: Police using AI risks making discrimination worse, researchers warn
summary: In his award-winning essay, young British science writer Adrian Dredge wrote about the potential pitfalls of AI and policing.
key_takeaways: In his award-winning essay, young British science writer Adrian Dredge wrote about the potential pitfalls of AI and policing.
The essay won the 2026 Young Science Writer Award , external , chosen each year by the Association of British Science Writers. Here is an ed
The growing use of AI in policing risks increasing discrimination against minority groups, researchers have warned.
content:
In his award-winning essay, young British science writer Adrian Dredge wrote about the potential pitfalls of AI and policing.

The essay won the 2026 Young Science Writer Award , external , chosen each year by the Association of British Science Writers. Here is an edited version of the entry.

The growing use of AI in policing risks increasing discrimination against minority groups, researchers have warned.

Studies suggest that predictions of future crime hotspots may be based on biased data, which can magnify existing prejudice and create a dangerous feedback loop.

Experts are calling for the use of AI in policing to be reviewed with greater human oversight.

This would involve checking the data that forces use to find and remove any bias, according to Dr Carolyn McKay, an associate professor and researcher in digital justice at the University of Sydney Law School.

"The public functions of state policing ought to be subject to human oversight and scrutiny," she says.

The problem, according to McKay, is that AI systems are trained on data that already contains human bias, and this can lead to self-fulfilling prophecies.

Think of AI as a map-maker asked to draw a map of a city they have never visited. They are locked in a windowless room and can't go outside. All they have are maps that are 50 years old.

Anyone following the new map would find themselves stopping at walls that were knocked down years ago and looking for roads that no longer exist. The map-maker hasn't made anything new. They have only copied the old maps.

Now suppose the map-maker is handed a list of past crimes and where they took place, and asked to shade in where the next ones are likely to happen. Police then patrol the shaded areas.

More crime is recorded there simply because more officers are there to see it. Areas outside the shading appear to have less crime, because fewer people are looking. When the next map is drawn, the same areas are shaded even darker.

So the crime figures are not a full list of crimes. They are partly a record of where police have chosen to look.

The problem is as old as policing, but AI may be speeding it up.

Sarah Brayne, a sociologist at the University of Texas at Austin, spent time inside the Los Angeles Police Department studying how it uses big data. In her research paper, published in the American Sociological Review, she found that the force increasingly used data to predict crime, rather than only to respond to it.

She also found that the data fed into these systems was skewed. Crimes in public places were more likely to be seen and recorded, and police focus was disproportionately on black neighbourhoods. Once this goes into the system, she writes, "the predictions appear impartial".

The models, she says, create "a feedback loop in which they not only predict events such as crime or police contact, but also contribute to their future occurrence."

But that is a view challenged by Dr Dimitrios Kollias, an associate professor in multimodal artificial intelligence at the Queen Mary University of London (QMUL). He says that the technology has moved on to take the bias of historical data into account.

"The old-map analogy is useful for explaining how historical bias can be inherited, but it has its limits," he told BBC News.

"Modern AI systems do not simply retrieve or copy their training examples; they can combine learned information in new ways and generate outputs and solutions that were not explicitly present in those examples."

But those new insights pose a separate risk, Kollias adds.

"As AI systems become more capable of generating novel decisions and acting with greater autonomy, we need to ensure that their behaviour remains safe, reliable and under meaningful human control," he said.

But arguably a more intractable problem is dealing with the sometimes flawed information stored by authorities and which AI systems draw from.

Researchers at New York University said that many of their predictions may rely on what they call "dirty data". These are police records shaped, they say, by corrupt, biased or unlawful practices, including rigged crime figures and arrests of innocent people.

In their study, the researchers found that in nine of the 13 US areas they looked at, police data from periods of unlawful or biased policing was available to train these systems.

The system can't tell that this data is flawed, according to the researchers. It simply treats it as a pattern to repeat. It is as if the map-maker's compass points only to where crime has been recorded before. The map-maker thinks they have found a new crime hotspot, when all they have done is follow the bias of earlier officers.

McKay's answer is to have someone independent check the map before anyone uses it and rub out the lines that are wrong.

But cleaning up dirty data won't be easy. The mistakes aren't a few stray pencil marks. The whole map has been drawn on top of them. The New York University researchers say that technical fixes offered by the companies selling these systems aren't enough unless someone independently checks how the data was produced in the first place.

Because AI can see the world only through the data it is given, it can make serious mistakes which can harm people.

For example, a 2019 study in the journal Science looked at an AI system used in US healthcare to help decide which patients should get extra support. It did this by predicting whose care would cost the most. But there was an inherent bias in the data it drew from. Less was already being spent on black patients than on equally ill white patients, partly because of poorer access to care. By treating higher costs as a sign of greater need, the system unfairly favoured white patients.

It was as if the map-maker had been told to mark the sickest parts of the city but had marked the places where the most money was spent instead. When the researchers changed the system to predict how ill patients were, rather than how much their care would cost, the bias largely disappeared. The share of black patients picked for extra help would have risen from about 18% to 47%.

Kollias acknowledges that AI bias from dirty data is "an important concern".

"But this does not mean that bias is inevitable." he says.

"We can test systems for unfair outcomes, improve the data and objectives they use, and introduce safeguards to reduce these effects."

One improvement would be to provide additional data that provides context. What if the map-maker were given more than a list of crimes? They could also be shown which areas have been neglected - places with broken streetlights, little funding and missing public services. That could show whether the local environment plays a part. Instead of sending police cars to the shaded areas, councils might send money to fix the lighting, support the community and repair the area itself.

Yet even this may not be enough, according to McKay.

"The target environments are still intimately linked with their inhabitants," she says. "They might (continue to) be over-policed and marginalised."

She points to systems which were designed to use information about places rather than people. Even so, critics raised concerns that they still led to over-policing.

title: Budget to include £1bn for social and affordable housing
summary: More than £1bn for social and affordable housing in England will be provided in the Budget, taking funding for the government's 10-year homes programme past £40bn.
key_takeaways: More than £1bn for social and affordable housing in England will be provided in the Budget, taking funding for the government's 10-year home
Mayors and regional leaders across England are also expected to get greater powers and funding in Wednesday's announcement - with councils h
It is hoped the plans will give regional leaders more flexibility and authority over investment decisions.
content:
More than £1bn for social and affordable housing in England will be provided in the Budget, taking funding for the government's 10-year homes programme past £40bn.

Mayors and regional leaders across England are also expected to get greater powers and funding in Wednesday's announcement - with councils helped to borrow money from the government to invest in house-building through preferential interest rates.

It is hoped the plans will give regional leaders more flexibility and authority over investment decisions.

Chancellor John Healey said English cities and regions would get the "right to decide their own future", while Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the plans were about shifting power to those "who know their communities best".

The chancellor will also announce more support for small breweries, with the Treasury saying he wants "to turn the tide for our pint producers".

Fresh support for breweries follows the news that 310 jobs are at risk at Marston's Brewery in Burton-upon-Trent.

The issue was raised again at Prime Minister's Questions earlier this week, after owners Carlsberg Britvic revealed plans to shut down operations at the historic brewing site.

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith has called for Healey to resign if he fails to set out how the UK will spend 3% of the UK's GDP on defence by 2030.

Published 2 days ago Between quick wins and big dreams lies Burnham's biggest test

Published 1 day ago Under the plans for the regions, an initial £285m in transitional seed funding will be allocated by the government next year to support mayors and local leaders - and reduce reliance on "fragmented bidding pots" in Whitehall, the Treasury said.

The government will also confirm that it will work with mayors to design a new £1.5bn borrowing facility from 2028, which would allow them to access capital needed to support local priorities.

The Treasury said this could be put towards new homes, bringing High Streets back to life, or improving transport links.

Healey said: "Mayors and local leaders know what their communities need to grow, which is why we are giving them more money, more power and more capacity to get projects moving, build homes and make the right decisions for their areas."

Areas across the country which are not yet strategic authorities will be able to access a share of the £285m to "unlock projects which will contribute to growth in their areas".

The prime minister said: "I'm calling time on local leaders going cap in hand to Westminster. That is no way to run a country."

Claire Ward, chairwoman of the UK Mayors Network and Labour's East Midlands mayor, said that having the "right powers and resources through increased devolution" would help turn "ambitious plans into reality and deliver real, lasting change" for communities.

Lord Sadiq Khan, Labour's mayor of London, said greater ability to invest could "help unlock transformational infrastructure projects" including the West London Orbital route, the extension of the Bakerloo Underground line and Docklands Light Railway, and the development of Stratford International station.

Departing Treasury entrepreneurship adviser, Alex Depledge, has criticised the government's treatment of start-ups ahead of her last day on Thursday - the day after the Budget.

She told the Sunday Times , external , that start-ups were being treated as a "sideshow" and should not be pushed to the "margins of economic policy".

"Keeping scale-ups on the fringes underestimates the contribution of our greatest companies, and we need to support and develop them on British shores at all costs," she said.

Leading up to the Budget, defence has also remained a key talking point. Healey resigned in June from his role as defence secretary in the previous government over the defence investment plan , which he claimed fell "well short" of what was needed to fund the armed forces.

He had called for defence spending to rise to 3% of the country's GDP by 2030, on the way to reaching a Nato target of 3.5% in 2035.

But urging him to commit to setting out plans to spend 3% of GDP on defence, the shadow chancellor said: "We are living in an era of extraordinary threats, and yet the chancellor is dithering over finding the money to pay the country's insurance premium... you cannot have a strong economy without a strong defence".

Responding to Andrew Griffith's comments, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the Conservatives were to blame for failing to invest in the military while in office.

Streeting said the prime minister had made it clear that his government was "determined to give our armed forces the investment needed to keep us safe".

The Metropolitan Police said officers were called to the scene at an address in St Paul's Road, Barking, at about 11:00 BST on Saturday morning, following reports that a child had fallen from height.

Paramedics from the London Ambulance Service gave first aid and the child was taken to hospital, but later died from her injuries.

"Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with the child's family and loved ones at this incredibly difficult time," they said.

content:
It is hardly a typical round for a postie, but for five months of the year George Clarke leaves behind his partner and friends in Bristol to become a postmaster at the world's most southerly post office - in Antarctica.

"I thought it sounded like an amazing experience - living away from home for a few months on a very small island with five other people and 1,000 penguins," says Clarke.

He takes up his role as Port Lockroy postmaster from late October to March, during the southern hemisphere summer.

The part-time festival worker and artist says his days are spent sorting postcards, processing letters and arranging for the post to hitch a ride north on passing ships before being distributed around the world.

"The penguins are noisy and smelly. The people are fantastic," he said. "I've fallen in love with the Antarctic wilderness."

When Clarke sets off with in a team of six on Monday, it will be his third voyage to Antarctica helping the UK Antarctic Heritage Trust (UKAHT) to conserve Port Lockroy, a former British science research facility.

Unlike a regular post office, there is no fleet of vans ready to whisk the mail away.

"When we collect up all the postcards and we've sorted through them, we've bagged them up, we've weighed them, we then need to look to see which ships are heading north towards the Falklands," he said.

"Then we get them on email or the radio and we say, 'Hello, would you mind taking some postcards with you?' And they're always very keen to oblige."

Published 1 day ago The rise of new black spaces in music

Published 20 hours ago Unsurprisingly, running a post office for six people does not take up all of Clarke's time at Port Lockroy.

He is also the deputy base commander, helps with the cleaning and maintenance of the site, and helps with wildlife observations for the British Antarctic Survey (BAS).

"The primary objective of the charity is conservation of the heritage surrounding UK exploration in Antarctica," Clarke said.

The team of six is about to embark on the second term of a three-year plan to shore-up and restore the island's largest building, Bransfield House, which is home to a museum, the post office and a shop.

They will install beams in the roof and 30 steel and timber props in the floor to help it withstand rain and snow.

The site on Goudier Island was chosen in the 1940s to become a permanent British foothold in Antarctica because it was known as a safe place to anchor by early 20th Century whaling ships.

The remnants of that industry are still clear to see, with the bones of whales killed long ago for their oil littering part of the shore.

Port Lockroy operated until 1962, when British research was moved to larger and more modern sites in Antarctica.

The journey from the UKAHT base in Cambridgeshire to Port Lockroy takes about a week.

"We fly to Ushuaia via Buenos Aires in Argentina and we'll probably have a couple of days to acclimatise slightly," Clarke said.

"We'll then jump on a ship that will take us south to the Antarctic Peninsula and it takes four or five days."

Clarke's colleagues are also excited to get the new season under way.

Base commander and RAF veteran Carole McCullough said: "I applied for the role looking for a bit of an adventure, and Antarctica is the ultimate adventure.

"The team work, the bonding, the appreciation of the place - it's all going to make for the most wonderful experience."

Wildlife monitor and museum manager Alice Parr added: "I actually applied for a role three years ago and was selected as reserve.

"I tried again - clearly persistence pays off! I'm incredibly excited to be managing the museum and counting penguins. It's the opportunity of a lifetime."

content:
Ukraine is in desperate need of a new satellite internet service, but a fast and reliable alternative to Elon Musk's Starlink network simply doesn't exist - yet.

Last week's sudden slowdown of the service in Ukraine, which affected Kyiv's ability to defend itself from Russian attacks, has shown how vulnerable the country can be, and sharply increased Europe's urgency to have its own military-grade satellite network.

That vulnerability was highlighted by Musk himself on Saturday, when he accused Ukraine of violating Starlink's terms of service by using it for "drone strikes to kill people".

Saying that loophole was closed last week, he wrote on X , external : "Violation of those terms will result in end of service."

He added: "Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately".

Published 15 October There are a few alternatives, but they are all lagging behind Starlink, which is the world's largest satellite constellation.

France's Eutelsat, with its OneWeb internet service, is the main alternative - but it only has about 600 active satellites, compared with Starlink's 10,000-plus.

The EU is working on a new network to rival Starlink, Iris², however it won't be up and running until 2029.

For Ukraine's troops on the ground, several of whom spoke anonymously to the BBC, reliable connectivity is the difference between life and death.

"God forbid they shut it off completely, it would be an absolute catastrophe," said one. "I don't give a damn how much an alternative costs when our lives are on the line."

For now, Ukraine's best bet is to join Govsatcom, the EU's satellite sharing network - but it cannot be used for military warfare like controlling drones.

Starlink and its military-grade service, Starshield, are both owned by Musk's SpaceX company and have dominated the global satellite market for years.

Ukraine relies on Starlink for communications on the battlefield and Starshield, which is controlled by the US government, for military purposes like drone warfare. The network is able to provide fast, real-time connectivity, which is crucial for defence and intercepting Russian attacks.

"You can't employ drone warfare without this kind of high-speed internet connection," said Vincent Tourret, a researcher at the French Institute of International Relations.

Last week's slowdown, which has only just been restored , highlighted the risks of relying on a US provider at a time when tensions between Kyiv and Washington continue to deteriorate.

"Ukraine's defence cannot depend on Trump's or Musk's whims," French MEP, Christophe Grudler, tweeted.

Who authorised the Starlink restrictions is still not clear, with a confusing blame-game ongoing between the Pentagon, Donald Trump and Musk.

While Starlink has been one of Ukraine's greatest assets in this conflict, the "flipside of that dependence" has been exposed, explained Kari Bingen, director of the Aerospace Security Project at CSIS.

"This is a critical military capability that Ukraine relies on, but doesn't control."

Starlink is not the only satellite network Ukraine can access, so if it goes down there are other options - but experts say they aren't as fast, and troops the BBC spoke to agree.

Starlink "gives us the upper hand when it comes to passing commands - even one or two seconds are critical when we can transfer data and orders faster, and you can really feel that advantage on the battlefield", a soldier said.

The terminals used to connect to the satellites are also an important factor. Starlink's are relatively small and lightweight, so they can be fixed to any kind of vehicle or drone.

Eutelsat's terminals "are slightly larger, so they can be fitted on the roof of a car, or on tanks, but they can't necessarily sit on small drones", said Eva Berneke, former CEO of the French satellite company.

They are also about five times more expensive, she added.

Rhetoric from the White House - like Trump's scathing criticism of Nato and his threats against Greenland - have given the EU "some pretty brutal alarm bells", Berneke told the BBC.

She had only been at Eutelsat for a month when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and said she noticed a marked change in urgency from European authorities, as they looked to her company to help plug holes left by Starlink if it could not be relied upon.

Comments from Musk have further heightened the need for an alternative: "Be quiet, small man... there is no substitute for Starlink," he tweeted , external at Poland's foreign minister last year, when the politician said he would "look for other suppliers" if SpaceX was unreliable.

Europe has realised its security depends on space, and it must "strengthen its satellite capacities, urgently", a spokesperson for the European Commission told the BBC.

Right now, it has Govsatcom, a network that was set up in January to share existing satellites between EU member states. Ukraine is not a full-fledged member (although it is trying to become one), but the Commission is in talks with Kyiv to join Govsatcom.

But even if Ukraine could connect tomorrow, the network could not be used for warfare operations like piloting drones, which Starshield is used for.

That could change by the start of next year, however, when the European Commission hopes commercial companies, like Eutelsat's OneWeb, will join the programme. This will give Ukraine some - but not all - of its military network needs.

Eva Berneke told the BBC she is confident the company will be able to "support quite a lot of Ukraine's key military needs". But meeting its communications needs is another thing because, as is the case with most countries, they are varied and massive.

Eutelsat could not comment on Govsatcom, but told the BBC that "as the only European operator of a fully operational [Low Earth Orbit] constellation, we are committed to providing resilient connectivity to the businesses, governments and communities we serve".

No timeline has been given for when Ukraine will be able to join the Govsatcom network. When it does it will likely be as a reliable back-up to Starlink and Starshield.

But that's better than nothing, Vincent Tourret said. "If Starlink is shut down, it's good to have another way to stay connected, but it won't be enough for strikes or interceptions, at this stage."

Govsatcom is seen as a short-term safety net, until the stronger and more secure network, Iris² , external is up and running in 2029.

The ambitious project (pronounced Iris squared ) is Europe's answer to Starlink and Starshield. It will be a defence-first programme, the European Commission says, with a focus on governments, military and emergency services. Ukraine has been guaranteed access to it from day one.

Part of the EU's space programme, the European satellite companies Eutelsat, SES and Hispasat are leading the project in a consortium called SpaceRISE.

It will still have far fewer satellites than Starlink, with 348 across low and medium earth orbit - but that shouldn't be seen as a negative, said Kari Bingen.

"Think about a flash light beaming down - those satellites will be able to cover a greater amount of the Earth, so you need fewer of them," she explained. "They're all trade offs - I would not take it as a negative, that Iris² is planning for less satellites."

Tourret was more sceptical: "It's no gamechanger and no great saviour, I'm afraid".

A highly produced video on the EU Space Policy's website declares: "With Iris², Europe will no longer depend on others for satellite connectivity."

So does that mean Ukraine could switch off Starlink? No - that wouldn't be a good idea.

"Users need to think about communications resilience," Bingen said. "So if something happens to one system, you have other ways to maintain connectivity."

title: A shark went astray and captured Korea's heart - will she finally make it back to sea?
summary: As soon as a large shark was spotted in a canal in Busan - a bustling shipping hub and beach city on South Korea's south-eastern tip - marine biologist Kim Hyun-woo was drafted in to rescue it.

content:
As soon as a large shark was spotted in a canal in Busan - a bustling shipping hub and beach city on South Korea's south-eastern tip - marine biologist Kim Hyun-woo was drafted in to rescue it.

He got the call in mid-September, on his way home from a business trip tracking shoals of mackerel to aid fishing vessels. Despite being one of the country's leading shark experts, he never thought he'd be asked by the coastguard to actually save one.

South Korea is no stranger to sharks but one this size, in a shallow, concrete canal right by the world's seventh busiest port, was unheard of - until now.

With an excited crowd already gathering at the waterfront, his team from the National Institute of Fisheries Science had to move fast.

Some sharks are more dangerous than others. The star of the 1975 blockbuster Jaws, the great white shark, is known to attack and kill humans.

The specimen in Busan was found to be a female dusky shark, a species linked only to two deadly attacks. Still, Kim feared someone in the crowd might jump or fall into the canal.

A small coastguard ship made an initial attempt using an electrical deterrence device, which generates a weak current that sharks avoid.

They're usually used after sightings near popular beaches. But after five hours, officials determined this particular shark was too large and fast for the device.

Kim changed tack, deciding instead to wait for the shark to let herself out. But that did not happen.

As authorities looked for ways to guide her out of the canal, the stranded creature went viral.

Just hours after she appeared, the council had sent everyone in the city an emergency text alert, urging pedestrians and residents to "exercise caution for their safety".

People rarely visited the park along the canal but because of the message, the place was soon brimming with people eager to spot the shark.

Adoring fans named her Bukangi, from "buk hang", the Korean name of the nearby harbour. Within days, a business trademarked it and Bukangi pins, plushies and T-shirts began selling online.

City authorities joined in, livestreaming the shark and making her their official mascot.

A banner was hung at the entrance of the canal, asking the public to sign a petition "on behalf of Bukangi" to demand the national government's support for the construction of a new 30,000-seater baseball stadium by the canal.

Shark spotting became a team effort among locals and visitors. The unspoken rule was that children were given the front row, and whoever saw Bukangi had to point her out to newer arrivals.

Some self-appointed defenders even patrolled the canal at night to make sure no-one was shining torches or lasers at Bukangi.

More than 1.6 million visitors ultimately flocked to the canal.

The local mayor said the shark brought "the kind of publicity even billions of dollars cannot buy" to the port.

"It's really rare these days for people to come together," said Kim Joo-eun, who came to see the shark with her two nieces. "I feel that Bukangi brought us all together, cheering for her… It's a lot of fun."

As September drew to an end, she hadn't been seen feeding for days and was spotted with bloody abrasions on her snout from bumping into the concrete walls.

Prominent marine biology professor Choi Yoon told local media that experts were particularly worried about a "critical" injury around the shark's eye.

At the end of September, Kim's team mounted another rescue attempt. The marine biologist looked back to a 2004 incident in Massachusetts, when water jets were used to drive a great white shark away from a shallow pond.

But when the team tried this on Bukangi, she kept circling back.

On 2 October, they decided to install a net spanning the width of the canal to stop her from returning. She managed to swim around the net and was back within hours.

At this point, Kim started thinking the shark might have problems with her snout's electromagnetic sensors, which she uses for navigation. Or she might have become confused by the loud noises emitted by ships in the harbour.

The reason Bukangi was even in the canal may be a sign of warming seas, the oceans ministry suggests.

It believes she may have followed plentiful fish to warmer waters. Some 50 large sharks were recorded off South Korea's east coast in the first half of the year; four times as many as last year.

With each failed attempt some of Bukangi's newfound fans began demanding she be left in peace.

On Thursday, several showed up with placards and shouted "leave Bukangi alone" and "remove the net".

When a security guard told them to stop, one man cried: "I love you, Bukangi!"

"I am obsessed with her," said Jeong Yo-won, a woman in her 40s. She called the shark a "source of hope and joy" and insisted, "I don't think we should evict her mercilessly like this."

"I would stare at her for hours because I was so enamoured by her," a woman said after sighting the shark on her third attempt. "I hope Bukangi would stay, but I prefer that she lives a long and healthy life."

People joked the council should "make an official ID for Bukangi and give a pension", Shin Seungmin said.

"She brought so much fun with her. But she should go and live her normal shark life."

Staying in the canal would seriously jeopardise Bukangi because of falling autumn temperatures, Kim explains. Usually this prompts sharks to migrate to warmer waters further south.

"This canal is far from something we can call a habitat," he adds. "A wild animal cannot stay in a space made strictly for humans."

Eventually, as public scrutiny grew, the oceans ministry took over the rescue operation from the fisheries institute. Around 40 personnel, including divers from Busan's aquarium, were mobilised. A vet was on standby, along with an ambulance in case the divers were attacked by Bukangi.

On Wednesday divers installed two layers of nets, and Bukangi was successfully herded out of the narrow canal into open water. But overnight, she swam back into the canal, diving under the outer net.

Then on thursday, rescuers removed the outer layer, and Bukangi was seen swimming further and further towards open sea.

Although she did occasionally circle back, the rescue operation had ended.

There have been no sightings of Bukangi in the last few days, which experts say is a positive sign.

Prof Choi believes she may be adjusting to wider, deeper waters.

She is unlikely to have travelled far, he adds, and could reappear over the coming week.

But he is also worried about any injuries she may have sustained. Trapped in the canal, it "kept scraping against [the walls], stripping the skin off its snout and even its pectoral fins", he told local media.

For now, South Korea is holding its breath, hoping Bukangi can find her way back to her home - the open sea.

title: Navigating the Fiscal Squeeze: Four Levers the Chancellor Could Pull to Balance the Books
summary: Confronted by evaporating fiscal headroom and strict manifesto pledges on headline taxes, the Treasury faces an acute budgetary dilemma. We examine the four alternative policy levers ministers could deploy to raise billions ahead of the fiscal statement.
key_takeaways: Treasury fiscal headroom has shrunk dramatically from £24bn to an estimated £11bn due to elevated debt servicing costs.
Targeted measures including a bank corporation tax surcharge, higher duties on gaming machines, and online marketplace VAT enforcement could generate roughly £3.5bn annually.
Reining in the escalating working-age welfare bill represents a larger fiscal prize but carries severe political and operational risks.
content:
As the Treasury finalises preparations for the upcoming Budget, intense scrutiny is falling upon the government's fiscal headroom—the thin margin of financial buffer required to satisfy self-imposed borrowing rules. Economists warn that this cushion has deteriorated markedly over the past six months, collapsing from roughly £24bn to as little as £11bn, largely driven by the heightened yield the British state must pay private debt investors amid persistent interest rates.

With ministers under pressure to protect defence commitments and alleviate cost-of-living distress, the Chancellor faces a formidable arithmetic challenge. The governing party’s election manifesto committed unequivocally to avoiding increases to the headline rates of income tax, Value Added Tax (VAT), and National Insurance, whilst potential windfalls from capital gains adjustments or residential property levies have faced administrative and political headwinds. Consequently, Whitehall has turned its focus toward narrower, structural measures capable of delivering revenue without breaching core pledges.

Chief among the options under contemplation is an enhanced surcharge on the banking sector. Having enjoyed bumper profits from elevated net interest margins in recent years, commercial lenders could see their corporation tax surcharge increased from 3% to 5.5%. Independent policy analysts calculate that this adjustment could furnish the Treasury with between £1bn and £2bn annually. However, the financial sector has cautioned that ratcheting up domestic levies risks disincentivising international capital, dampening lending capacity, and denting returns for institutional pension funds.

Simultaneously, fiscal planners are reviewing levies on electronic gaming machines across betting shops and high-street adult gaming venues. Raising duties on high-stake terminals from 20% to 40% could yield up to £460m, framed by public health advocates as a necessary step to curb addictive gambling harms clustered disproportionately in economically deprived neighbourhoods. The bookmaking sector, conversely, warns that punitive duties would shutter retail shops and deplete statutory contributions to British horseracing.

A third structural intervention targets the so-called 'VAT gap', particularly within cross-border e-commerce. Proposed regulations would compel major online marketplaces such as Amazon, eBay, and Temu to assume direct liability for collecting and remitting VAT generated by third-party merchants on their platforms. While enforcement has historically been hampered by overseas vendors obscuring their origins or liquidating shell entities to dodge liabilities, shifting the compliance burden onto digital platform operators could capture up to £1bn in lost state revenue each year.

Yet, even combined, these tax mechanisms would raise only around £3.5bn annually—a fraction of the capital required to decisively stabilise public accounts. This arithmetic puts the welfare budget squarely under the spotlight. Expenditure on working-age health and incapacity benefits is forecast to climb from £68bn to £81bn by the end of the decade. While opposition figures and fiscal hawks advocate aggressive entitlement rollbacks, previous administrative attempts to compress disability spending triggered fierce parliamentary resistance. Experts note that genuinely reducing the claimant count requires substantial upfront capital in vocational and occupational healthcare support, meaning immediate savings may prove elusive.
why_it_matters: The British fiscal strategy serves as an acute case study for developed economies grappling with post-pandemic debt burdens, elevated interest rates, and rigid political constraints on broad-based taxation. How the Treasury balances revenue-raising with capital competitiveness and social safety provisions will signal whether mid-sized economies can maintain fiscal discipline without stunting structural growth.

title: British Mother Drowns in the Bahamas After Saving Her Sons from Sudden Riptide
summary: A Nottinghamshire mother has died after heroically rescuing her two young sons who were caught in a riptide during an anniversary holiday in the Bahamas. Her husband has paid tribute to his childhood sweetheart, describing her as a hero who gave her life to save her children.
key_takeaways: Leanne Gregory, 36, from Stapleford, Nottinghamshire, drowned off the island of Bimini whilst rescuing her two sons from a powerful current.
The couple were marking an early celebration of their 10th wedding anniversary when the sudden tragedy unfolded in under ten minutes.
Local police confirmed the two boys survived without serious injury, while the Foreign Office has pledged ongoing consular support to the family.
content:
A British mother has died after braving treacherous waters to rescue her two young sons who had been swept out to sea during a family holiday in the Bahamas.

Leanne Gregory, 36, from Stapleford in Nottinghamshire, was visiting the Caribbean archipelago with her husband, Nathan, and their children to mark an early celebration of their forthcoming tenth wedding anniversary. The trip turned to tragedy off the coast of North Bimini when their sons, who were snorkelling in shallow water, were suddenly dragged into deeper waters by a severe riptide.

Recounting the incident, Mr Gregory explained that the boys had been enjoying the shallows as their parents organised bags on the beach. Upon realising the children were in distress, both parents immediately entered the sea to pull them to safety. The entire harrowing ordeal unfolded in less than ten minutes. While the two boys were successfully retrieved from the ocean, Mrs Gregory succumbed to the conditions.

Emergency services were alerted shortly after 10:00 local time on Tuesday. The Royal Bahamas Police Force confirmed that Mrs Gregory was recovered from the water and brought to the North Bimini Ferry Dock, where cardiopulmonary resuscitation was administered. She was transported to a nearby medical clinic but was pronounced dead shortly after arrival. Authorities stated that an autopsy will be conducted, though foul play has been ruled out.

Paying tribute to his wife, whom he had known since primary school, Mr Gregory praised her selfless devotion to their family. He described her as the cornerstone of their household and an extraordinary figure who acted as a hero in both life and death. The couple had been together for 22 years, having first met as adolescents.

In the wake of the tragedy, neighbours and local representatives in Nottinghamshire have rallied behind the bereaved family. Local community figures noted that the tight-knit town of Stapleford has been deeply moved by the loss, with an online fundraiser amassing thousands of pounds to support the family through the aftermath. A spokesperson for the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office affirmed that consular assistance is actively being provided in coordination with Bahamian authorities.
why_it_matters: This tragic incident serves as a poignant reminder of the unpredictable hazards posed by coastal currents, even in popular tourist destinations known for calm waters. It underscores the critical need for heightened water-safety vigilance and rapid response infrastructure on recreational beaches, whilst highlighting the profound vulnerability travellers face abroad when sudden natural perils occur.

title: Conscription Crisis: The Deepening Divide Threatening Israel's Political Future
summary: Simmering anger over military exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men has reached boiling point across Israel as fighting continues on multiple fronts. With the Supreme Court striking down draft relief, the contentious dispute threatens to reshape national identity and topple fragile political alliances.
content:
Furious demonstrators have denounced security forces on Israeli streets, but these scenes are not anti-war protests in European capitals. Instead, the clashes represent a bitter domestic confrontation in the heart of Israel, where hundreds of ultra-Orthodox men dressed in traditional white shirts and black coats have faced off directly against military police.

The flashpoint was an apartment block in the city of Modi'in, positioned between Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, home to a young ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, man. Police arrived to detain him after he failed to report for mandatory military service, triggering fierce street protests—one of dozens of similar incidents exposing one of the most volatile fractures in Israeli society.

This widening schism comes against the backdrop of protracted conflict in Gaza and surging instability in the region. Once a small minority composed largely of Holocaust survivors granted military exemptions to preserve traditional scholarship, the Haredi population has expanded rapidly. Today, ultra-Orthodox Jews make up roughly 14% of the population, with high birth rates projecting they could constitute a third of the Jewish Israeli public by 2050.

Alongside this demographic shift, resentment has grown over the substantial public funds required to support full-time religious scholars. State stipends and subsidies are estimated to cost the treasury 35 billion shekels (£8.4bn) annually. As the community expands, secular and modern Orthodox Israelis increasingly demand that Haredi men contribute equally to the nation's security and tax base.

The debate has intensified considerably since the outbreak of war following the 7 October attacks. With the Israel Defense Forces facing severe personnel shortages and reservists enduring hundreds of days of frontline duty, the traditional blanket exemption for religious seminarians, or yeshivas, has provoked profound public fury.

Rabbinical authorities within the Haredi establishment maintain that rigorous Torah study provides spiritual defence essential to Israel's survival. Senior religious leaders have warned that enlisting would expose young men to secular influences, eroding centuries of faith traditions. Some prominent rabbis have gone so far as to instruct students neither to enlist nor even attend military funerals.

However, wider public patience has run out. Opinion polls indicate overwhelming support for ending the exemption, not only among political centrists and left-wing voters, but crucially across the religious-nationalist right, whose communities have borne a heavy proportion of military casualties.

A landmark ruling by Israel's Supreme Court declared the military exemption unlawful, leaving the government legally obligated to begin conscription. The move sparked massive demonstrations, with thousands blocking arterial roads to resist arrests.

The impasse carries severe political consequences for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Dependent on ultra-Orthodox factions—such as United Torah Judaism and Shas—to maintain his parliamentary majority, the prime minister faces a perilous dilemma: enforcing conscription risks collapsing his coalition, while delaying it fuels fury among an exhausted and combat-weary electorate.

title: Why the Music Charts and Our Playlists Are Full of Old Songs
summary: Listeners are turning away from new releases as back-catalogue hits and algorithmic nostalgia dominate the streaming charts. The shift presents growing hurdles for emerging musicians struggling to find long-term audiences.
content:
More music is being produced today than at any other point in human history, with upwards of 100,000 new tracks uploaded to streaming platforms daily. Yet, despite this unprecedented deluge of material, listeners are increasingly turning backwards rather than embracing the new.

Data from entertainment analytics company Luminate reveals that the consumption of current music—defined as material released within the past 18 months—is being heavily eclipsed by older recordings. Across both the UK and the US, roughly 60% of all streams now belong to songs released five or more years ago.

In the UK, the phenomenon is stark. Eighteen of the year's top 20 bestselling tracks were originally released at least 12 months ago. Decade-old hits such as Zara Larsson's 2015 single Lush Life, Michael Jackson's 1983 classic Billie Jean, and Fleetwood Mac's Dreams from 1977 routinely rub shoulders with current chart-toppers. In heavily streamed genres like R&B and hip-hop, around 60% of listening belongs to what the industry categorises as "deep catalogue".

Even when new songs succeed, they linger at the summit for unprecedented periods. Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's collaborative single Rein Me In recently set a record by spending 23 non-consecutive weeks at number one in the UK, while in the United States, Ella Langley's Choosin' Texas achieved a similar historic run. According to the UK's Competition and Markets Authority, nearly two-thirds of all streams belong to just the top 0.4% of artists.

This consolidation has left aspiring artists in a precarious position. The fleeting nature of social media virality rarely translates into enduring careers. As J Erving, founder of distribution company Human Re Sources, recently observed, platforms such as TikTok tend to foster passive fandom built around isolated clips rather than genuine connections with artists.

The broader music ecosystem is attempting to respond. Streaming executives note the imperative to cultivate future headline talent who can sustain arena tours decades from now, while grassroots organisations like Sofar Sounds are promoting live, intimate gigs and bespoke human curation to break the cycle of automated listening.

Algorithmic playlisting and artificial intelligence are also coming under scrutiny. Streaming giants have introduced prompt-based curation that generates playlists tailored to specific moods, but experts warn this creates echo chambers. Musicologist Anna-Kaisa Kaila points out that recommendation models rely on existing consumption habits, systematically penalising less commercially prominent genres and emergent acts.

Independent artists further caution that automated ambient playlists are increasingly populated by unverified accounts and formulaic, mass-produced tracks that capture millions of passive streams. While major streaming companies maintain they are cracking down on spam and deceptive practices, the battle for listeners' attention remains tilted firmly towards the familiar.

title: Inside Rosebank: Life on the North Atlantic oil field at the centre of a political storm
summary: Moored amid treacherous swells west of Shetland, the Petrojarl Rosebank vessel is ready to extract millions of barrels of oil. But as the UK government weighs final approval, the project remains caught between energy security ambitions and fierce climate opposition.
content:
Eighty miles north-west of Shetland, in one of the world's most unforgiving stretches of ocean, a mammoth vessel rolls gently against the North Atlantic swell. The Petrojarl Rosebank, a floating production, storage and offloading vessel (FPSO), sits in waiting above Britain's largest known untapped oil field.

Here, amid sub-zero gales and waves that can reach up to 30 metres, an intense national debate over climate change, economic survival and energy security plays out in real time. The field beneath holds an estimated 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil and gas—enough to sustain production for a quarter of a century.

For the 122 crew members living and working aboard the vessel, life is dictated by a strict offshore rhythm. Shifts run round the clock amidst a dizzying maze of pipes, valves and heavy steelwork. Despite the ferocious conditions outside, the living quarters offer modern comforts, from single-occupancy en-suite cabins and saunas to extensive recreation suites.

Operating West of Shetland requires exceptional engineering and resilience. Unlike fixed platforms in calmer waters, the Rosebank vessel is designed to rotate around a central turret, continuously turning to face into the prevailing weather. If operations are fully sanctioned, crude oil will be pumped through this turret, held in the hull, and transferred via massive marine hoses directly onto export tankers.

The project, owned by Ithaca and Adura—a joint venture between Shell and Norway's state energy giant Equinor—has become a key battleground. Regulators first granted development consent in 2023, but environmental groups challenged the decision in court. In a landmark ruling, the Scottish Court of Session judged the initial permits unlawful because authorities had failed to assess the environmental impact of burning the extracted fossil fuels.

Campaigners insist that approving Rosebank would be disastrous for emissions targets, arguing that the majority of the extracted oil will be traded on international markets rather than directly benefiting domestic consumers. They argue that government policy should focus exclusively on renewable energy infrastructure.

Developers and offshore workers counter that domestic extraction remains vital during the green transition. Proponents note that the field will also yield gas, which will be piped directly into the national grid via Aberdeenshire, providing enough fuel to heat an estimated 500,000 households at peak output, while generating substantial tax revenues for the public purse.

With production decisions pending, Rosebank stands as the focal point of a wider dilemma facing Britain: how to balance the realities of a declining domestic energy basin with the pressing demands of net-zero obligations.

title: Brazilians vote in tense presidential run-off as Lula faces Bolsonaro's son
summary: Voters across Brazil are heading to the polls in a pivotal presidential run-off between veteran left-wing incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing senator Flávio Bolsonaro. The high-stakes contest follows a strong first-round performance by Bolsonaro, testing Lula's political resilience.
content:
Polls have opened across Brazil as citizens cast their ballots in a fiercely contested presidential run-off election that will define the political trajectory of Latin America's largest nation.

The contest pits 80-year-old incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a veteran leftist seeking a fourth non-consecutive term in office, against 45-year-old right-wing senator Flávio Bolsonaro. The challenger is the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence under house arrest for his involvement in a coup plot following the 2022 election.

Flávio Bolsonaro entered Sunday's vote holding a decisive advantage after topping the initial ballot on 4 October. Historically, no presidential candidate in Brazil has ever overturned a first-round deficit to secure victory in the second round.

Casting his vote in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday morning alongside his wife, Senator Bolsonaro declared that the "time has come for real change". His campaign platform has focused heavily on law and order, promising a sweeping crackdown on organised crime alongside cuts to public spending and taxation. He has also pledged to grant a pardon to his father, who remains confined to his residence in Brasília owing to deteriorating health.

Meanwhile, Lula and his Workers' Party have framed the contest as a fundamental defence of Brazilian democracy, cautioning voters that the resurgence of "Bolsonarismo" poses an existential threat to democratic institutions. In the days leading up to the vote, Lula staged massive rallies aimed at galvanising the 33 million electors who abstained in the first round.

Addressing a sea of supporters on Rio's Copacabana beach, Lula presented the election as a battle for national sovereignty. He pointedly contrasted his vision with that of his rival, whom he accused of deference to Washington. Diplomatic relations between Brasília and the White House have grown strained during Lula's tenure, with the Brazilian leader insisting his country "does not fit into anyone's backyard".

In contrast, Bolsonaro has advocated closer cooperation with the United States to dismantle transnational narcotics gangs, arguing that federal authority must be restored in areas dominated by armed factions. He has also revived accusations of past corruption against the Workers' Party, a narrative that continues to resonate with large swathes of the electorate.

Lula is scheduled to monitor the election returns from São Paulo, while Bolsonaro will await the results in the capital, Brasília, where the nation braces for an outcome that will reshape its domestic and international standing.

title: Why the King's Caribbean tour marks the biggest gamble of his reign
summary: King Charles III is embarking on an intensive nine-day tour of the Caribbean amid mounting debate over slavery reparations and republicanism. The visit carries significant diplomatic and personal stakes as the monarch seeks to balance royal duties with historical sensitivities.
content:
Royal tours are notoriously unpredictable endeavours. Months, often years, of meticulous planning can quickly be overshadowed by the shifting political winds of the modern Commonwealth.

King Charles III's latest overseas visit takes him to three Caribbean nations in nine days: the Bahamas, Guyana, and Antigua and Barbuda, where he will attend the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm). The high-profile trip thrusts the monarch directly into the intensifying debate surrounding reparatory justice for the transatlantic slave trade, alongside renewed questions about whether the Crown should issue a formal apology for its historic involvement.

Historian and author Sir Anthony Seldon described the voyage as "the biggest risk of his reign so far", noting that fundamental questions surrounding slavery, reparations, and apologies place the moral standing of the monarchy under sharp international scrutiny.

The King is scheduled to deliver three major speeches during the visit. In line with established ministerial advice, he will not offer a formal state apology, as UK government policy maintains that reparations will not be paid. However, a senior royal aide indicated that the monarch would "not shy away from the darkest days of our past", while emphasising that decisions regarding official apologies and financial compensation remain matters for elected politicians.

Buckingham Palace has incorporated acknowledgements of historical wrongs into the official itinerary across all three nations. Nevertheless, calls for republicanism and reparations are expected to draw demonstrations. Organisers view peaceful dissent as an inevitable feature of healthy, vibrant democracies and have integrated protests into their logistical planning.

Palace officials will be particularly keen to avoid the public relations missteps of the 2022 Caribbean tour undertaken by the Prince and Princess of Wales, when awkward photographic optics and local protests prompted widespread criticism.

While political leaders in the Bahamas, Guyana, and Antigua and Barbuda have expressed their commitment to reparatory justice, they are also set to highlight the King's longstanding advocacy for environmental protection, rainforest conservation, and bilateral trade. In Antigua and Barbuda and the Bahamas, where Charles III remains head of state, the transition toward a republic continues to gather momentum, with local authorities already having phased out mandatory oaths of allegiance to the Crown.

The diplomatic test comes against a demanding physical backdrop. At nearly 78 years of age and continuing regular treatment following his cancer diagnosis earlier this year, the King faces an arduous programme of roughly three dozen engagements. Buckingham Palace has reiterated that his medical trajectory remains positive, with Queen Camilla scheduled to join him for the final leg in Antigua and Barbuda.

If navigated successfully, the tour could reinforce the King's reputation as a modernising and empathetic head of the Commonwealth, demonstrating an ability to address complex historical legacies with diplomacy and resolve.

title: More than 1,300 arrested as fresh clashes hit France after mass protests
summary: Police have arrested more than 1,300 people across France following another day of widespread demonstrations over the cost of living. While daytime marches were largely peaceful, nightfall brought violent clashes, barricade fires, and tear gas across several major cities.
content:
More than 1,300 people have been arrested across France after hundreds of thousands took part in a fresh wave of nationwide protests that were followed by sporadic clashes, according to official figures.

While daytime demonstrations remained broadly peaceful, riot police deployed tear gas and water cannon as night fell to disperse groups in several cities, including Paris, Marseille, and Bordeaux. Makeshift barricades were torched and shopfronts damaged, though authorities managed to avert the widespread looting seen the previous weekend.

The interior ministry estimated that 410,000 people took to the streets on Saturday, while trade union organisers placed the turnout considerably higher, at around 800,000. Approximately 70,000 police officers had been mobilised nationwide to prevent a repeat of recent unrest, which saw hundreds of businesses ransacked and public buildings attacked.

Officials confirmed that 53 officers were injured during Saturday's disturbances. French President Emmanuel Macron had earlier decreed that only marches coordinated by recognised trade unions would be authorised, following fast-track judicial hearings that saw hundreds jailed in connection with earlier unrest.

In Paris, confrontations erupted near the end of a march between Porte d'Italie and Porte de Vincennes. Masked youths smashed the windows of a car showroom and hurled projectiles at security forces, prompting baton charges from specialised units. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez noted that several thousand radical activists had embedded themselves at the rear of the procession, though the capital's arrest tally of 142 was less than half that recorded the previous week.

Similar disturbances were reported in other regional hubs. In the southern port city of Marseille, rubbish bins were ignited and metal hoardings used to erect street barricades, with local officials reporting damage to seven businesses. In Lyon, officers fired tear gas to break up an unauthorised assembly of students, while in Bordeaux, protesters used wooden boards torn from buildings to obstruct roads.

Mr Nuñez also reported that two people had suffered severe injuries during the day's events, including a 20-year-old demonstrator in Toulouse whose hand was badly damaged by an explosive device.

Public anger has been fuelled by soaring living costs, public sector cuts, and broader discontent with the current administration. Many participants described deep frustration with government policy, pointing to economic hardship and heavy taxation as the primary drivers of the sustained unrest.

The turmoil unfolds amid a sharply divided political climate, with France heading towards what is anticipated to be a fiercely contested general election. Opposition figures from both the hard-right National Rally and the radical-left La France Insoumise have heavily criticised the government's handling of the crisis, as public anger over living standards continues to spill onto the streets.

title: Andy Burnham calls for 'honest debate' on return to EU free movement
summary: Andy Burnham has indicated openness to discussing the restoration of free movement between the UK and the European Union. Opposition leaders have quickly criticised the suggestion, while senior allies maintain that all options should be explored to secure the best economic outcome.
content:
Andy Burnham has said he would welcome an "honest discussion" regarding the potential return of free movement between the United Kingdom and the European Union.

Speaking to the Sunday Times, he suggested that forging a closer relationship with Brussels could realistically include full EU membership or joining the single market, both of which would require freedom of movement.

Labour previously committed in its 2024 general election manifesto to ruling out a return to free movement, the single market or a customs union. Burnham indicated that any fundamental shift in policy would require a mandate from the public at the next general election.

"I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this," he said, arguing that the nature of migration has shifted since the 2016 referendum. "Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed... I think we've just got to have an honest discussion about those things."

However, he drew a clear boundary at monetary and border arrangements, stating: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."

Deputy Prime Minister Angela Rayner backed the principle of open dialogue, stating that "you can't take anything off the table" when seeking the best arrangement for the country. She noted that voters deserved a transparent assessment of the trade-offs involved before any future electoral decision.

Opposition parties reacted swiftly to the prospect. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch claimed the proposal demonstrated a fundamental misunderstanding of the public mood, arguing that ending free movement was a primary motivator for the Brexit vote.

Reform UK economy spokesperson Robert Jenrick also rejected the notion, describing the idea that Britain requires higher immigration as "mad" and asserting that large-scale migration had harmed British workers by undercutting wages.

By contrast, the Liberal Democrats welcomed the prospect of closer ties. Deputy leader Daisy Cooper argued that restoring free movement would act as an engine for economic growth, while urging the government to pursue membership of both the single market and the customs union.

title: Elon Musk admits SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink connection
summary: SpaceX boss Elon Musk has confirmed his company restricted Ukraine's access to Starlink satellite internet, accusing Kyiv of using the commercial network for offensive drone strikes. The admission follows days of operational disruption for Ukrainian forces before connectivity was reportedly restored.
content:
Elon Musk has confirmed that SpaceX intentionally curbed Ukraine's access to its Starlink satellite internet network, claiming the country's armed forces breached the service's terms of use.

The tech billionaire said the civilian communications network was restricted because it had been deployed to carry out offensive drone operations. His comments follow days of disruption reported by Ukrainian commanders, who said the sudden throttling had severely hindered defensive operations on the frontline.

Writing on social media platform X, Mr Musk insisted that commercial Starlink was never meant to be weaponised. "Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," he said, adding that a "loophole was closed last week". He maintained that Starshield, a separate military-grade satellite system run in partnership with the US government, remained under Washington's control.

Ukrainian officials expressed scepticism over Mr Musk's explanation. Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian presidency, described the billionaire's statement as "very strange", noting that technical restrictions already prevented commercial Starlink from operating on Russian soil or at high speeds required for deep-strike drones.

Connectivity has since improved, with Ukraine's Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara confirming that military units were once again registering stable connections. President Volodymyr Zelensky also noted that operational speeds were back to standard requirements.

The satellite row coincided with heightened diplomatic strain between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian drone attacks against Russian oil refineries. US President Donald Trump, who has urged Kyiv to halt refinery strikes amid global energy price pressures, said he had directly spoken to Mr Musk and told him to "put it back".

Starlink has been critical to Ukraine's war effort since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, enabling troops to coordinate battlefield communications across areas where conventional infrastructure has been obliterated.

title: Duchess of Sussex severed ties with father citing abuse claims, reports reveal
summary: The Duchess of Sussex permanently broke off contact with her father, Thomas Markle, in a letter citing allegations of child sexual abuse, sources indicate. Authorities in the Philippines and the US are now examining the claims, which Mr Markle strongly denies.
content:
The Duchess of Sussex permanently broke off contact with her father last year, informing him that both she and the authorities were aware of allegations that he had abused young girls.

Sources close to the duchess confirmed that Meghan sent a letter to Thomas Markle warning him that he would never meet his grandchildren, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, and making it clear she would not communicate with him again.

It is understood the letter was sent to Mr Markle, 82, while he was in hospital in the Philippines recovering from a leg amputation. The correspondence appears to mark a definitive conclusion to what has been an intensely strained relationship since 2018, when he withdrew from attending her wedding to Prince Harry citing health complications.

The development follows reports that illicit material, including child abuse images, was allegedly discovered among Mr Markle's possessions at his former residence in the Philippines. Mr Markle, who is currently undergoing rehabilitation in the United States, vehemently denies all allegations, rejecting claims that he ever possessed child sexual abuse images or engaged with underage individuals.

Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jnr, claimed he uncovered abuse images and videos while sorting through his father's belongings in the Philippines. He reported the discovery to the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) in July, an agency that has since confirmed awareness of the matter. Speaking to the press, Markle Jnr expressed remorse for having supported his father during the protracted family estrangement.

Authorities in the Philippines have launched an inquiry into the allegations. Officials confirmed that an anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force is investigating, while national police have seized Mr Markle's computer for digital forensic analysis.
